doc.title: George Russell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Touring the South with the Wilberforce Singers
summary: As drummer with the Wilberforce Singers he sang in swamp churches and met a preacher who milked rattlesnakes; they discuss Wilberforce's church and state character.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You mentioned that you were – one of your trips you were with the Wilberforce Singers. You were drumming, playing the drums for them?

Yeah. That’s when I got the taste of what the South then was really like, especially when we – we sang in – I remember we sang in small churches, in black churches in the swamps. I remember asking one man, who you couldn’t tell if he was black or white, where we stayed – I remember asking him, “What is God?” He said, “God is big.” Someone asked him, “How do you make a living here?” He went out into the field, came back with a rattler in his hand. “This is how I make my living.” He extracted from the snake the . . .
The skin with the rattle on it.
Did he – what did he do with those? He sell them? Or was he a mojo worker?
I don’t think – I think he had a way of going into the snake’s mouth and drawing something out of the snake.
Getting the venom? Milk the snake, as they say?
Yeah, and putting the snake back in the woods. Needless to say, I didn’t take a walk in the woods.
Sounds like he was a mojo man.
But he was a preacher. Looked more like a Latino than black.
Wilberforce was a church school, if I’m not mistaken.
Um-hmm. I think it was church-based, originally.
One part is a church, the other’s state. It’s state run and church run.
